headline: Cockenoe on the Last of the Ebb: Bluefish Come Back to the Deep Reef
subhead: After a dead July, blues are stacking on the drop-offs again — stripers are there too, but you have to grind for them.
body_markdown:
I picked Cockenoe on purpose this week, not Penfield, and not because it's my default August spot. Cockenoe's north side has that long rocky shelf that drops from eight feet down to twenty-eight in about sixty yards, and on the last two hours of the ebb that shelf turns into a funnel. Bait gets swept off the flat, piles up right at the lip of the drop, and anything hunting knows exactly where to look. That's where I found the bluefish again — and after a quiet July on this stretch of the Sound, that mattered.

The blues showed up exactly where the deep structure sets up: the outside edge of Cockenoe, the rockpile drop-off south of Penfield Reef, and the deeper contour lines running off Sheffield Island. These aren't the shoreline snappers you're fending off with poppers all summer — this is a better class of fish, mid-teens on the scale for a few of them, holding tighter to structure than you'd expect for bluefish. Diamond jigs in half-ounce and one-ounce, worked with a jigging motion off bottom on the last of the ebb, got bit consistently. If you've got poppers, work the surface at first light before the boat traffic starts — Cockenoe gets crowded fast on a summer Saturday, and once the wake traffic starts crossing that shelf, the bite shuts down. Early or late, that's the window.

We flagged this pattern last week — said building tidal flow into the August 12th new moon would sharpen the bite at current-driven structure, and that's exactly what showed up. The tidal range is stretching out day by day as we run up on the new moon, and every reef in this system that depends on current — Cockenoe, Penfield, the ledges off Greenwich Point — is starting to fish harder on both the ebb and the flood instead of just sitting dead on the tide change.

Stripers are around, but I won't oversell it. The pattern out here is what it's been most of the summer — you find them at night, deep, and mostly on the move. A few better fish, 40-plus pounds, have come off the west end near Greenwich Point on plastic eels fished slow along bottom, dead-sticked on the drift through the last hour of the flood into the first hour of the ebb. That's a tight window and it's not a volume game. If you want numbers instead of size, work the Cows off Stamford at night with bucktails tipped with a swimming mullet trailer, working the deeper mud-and-rock bottom in twenty-five to thirty-five feet. You'll get schoolies mixed with the occasional keeper, but you have to put in the hours after dark — daytime action on bass has been thin with this water warm and this much pleasure-boat pressure running over the reefs.

Fluke are the frustrating part of the report right now. Western Sound fluke have been small and scattered all summer, and this week didn't change that. I worked the channels between the Norwalk Islands — the deeper cuts around Sheffield and the flats off the back side — dragging white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter-ounce bucktails, and I covered a lot of water for a handful of shorts and one fish that just cleared the ruler. If you're set on fluke, fish the deeper water on the last of the outgoing where current concentrates bait against the channel edges, and don't expect a fast bag.

Porgies are the one thing out here that's been dependable without any qualifiers. The Cows off Stamford are thick with them in thirty to forty feet of water over that mixed mud-and-rock bottom — sandworms or clam on a simple high-low rig, fished on the slack ahead of the ebb, will load the cooler. It's not glamorous fishing but it's steady, and it's a good option on a day when the wind's up and you don't want to fight the open reefs.

Black sea bass are holding up well on the rockpiles around Sheffield Island and the deeper structure off Penfield — squid strips or Gulp on a jighead worked slow along bottom in twenty-five to thirty feet is putting keepers in the box, and that pattern should hold with little change through the rest of August. Blackfish are still off the table here — CT's summer closure keeps tog protected through spawning, and I wouldn't waste time targeting them until the season reopens later this month. Worth scouting the rockpiles now, though, so you know exactly where to drop once it's legal.

Looking ahead, the building tide into the August 12th new moon should keep sharpening the current-driven spots — expect the bluefish bite on the deep reef edges to hold or improve as bait keeps getting pushed off the flats on stronger ebbs. Stripers should stay a night pattern until water temps ease later in the month. If I had one day this week, I'd fish Cockenoe at first light on the ebb before the boat traffic arrives, then slide over to the Cows for porgies once the sun's up and the reef bite cools off. That's a realistic day, not a guaranteed one — but it's where the structure and the tide line up right now.
